items.rss_description: Independent Insurance Agencies in 2030 Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Thu, 11/05/2026 - 10:59 Independent insurance agencies face mounting operational inefficiencies, but agentic AI could unlock $4.7 billion in productivity gains by 2030. November 18, 2026 Image Independent insurance agencies, the backbone of personalized coverage in the U.S., are under siege from a perfect storm of operational inefficiencies, economic headwinds, regulatory shifts, environmental risks, and relentless consolidation. From 2022 to 2025, agencies grappled with inefficiencies costing 20-30% of annual revenue—translating to $200,000-$300,000 in lost profits for a mid-sized firm generating $1 million in premiums. Key performance indicators (KPIs) like customer acquisition cost (CAC) ballooned to $900 on average, while revenue per agent stagnated at $400,000-$500,000, eroding return on investment (ROI) and return on ad spending (ROAS) as retention rates slid below 85%. Looking ahead to 2030, these pain points will intensify: climate-driven premium hikes could add 22% to costs in high-risk regions like Florida and Louisiana, consolidation may swallow 20% more independents, and economic volatility from inflation and geopolitics could push expense ratios above 40%. Our forecasts project CAC rising 15-20% annually in coastal states, with revenue per employee dropping 10% due to talent shortages and tech lags. Yet, hope lies in agentic and generative AI voice and productivity agents like our Evolve AI Agent. Today, these tools slash claims processing time by 40%, boosting productivity and cutting CAC by 25%. By 2030, advances in multi-agent systems and real-time voice analytics will automate 60% of workflows, potentially unlocking $4.7 billion in AI-driven premiums industry-wide and restoring ROAS to 4:1 ratios. Pain Points From 2022-2025 The past three years have been a crucible for independent insurance agencies, marked by post-pandemic recovery, inflationary pressures, and accelerating digital disruption. Our proprietary research, corroborated by industry benchmarks, reveals operational inefficiencies as the primary culprit, draining resources and stifling growth. Agencies reported average monthly revenue losses of $16,667 (20% of $1M annual revenue benchmark), equating to $200,000 annually per firm, largely from manual processes and outdated systems. Operational Inefficiencies and Associated Costs At the core are legacy workflows: manual policy renewals, claims tracking, and commission reconciliation consume 30-40 hours per agent weekly, per our surveys. A 2023 IDC study pegs these inefficiencies at 20-30% of revenue lost yearly, or $2,000-$3,000 monthly per employee in wasted time (valued at $50/hour). Inefficiencies in distribution—such as siloed data and lengthy sales cycles—exacerbate this, leading to 20% lost revenue overall. For a 10-agent agency, this translates to $400,000 in annual opportunity costs, including negative ROAS from underperforming digital leads (often below 2:1 due to poor targeting). Customer expectations shifted dramatically post-2022, with 80% demanding digital-first service (PwC). Yet, 67% of executives cited data quality issues as barriers, per Deloitte, resulting in inconsistent reporting and 13-point drops in satisfaction scores. This churn costs agencies $5,000-$10,000 per lost client annually in foregone renewals. Talent woes compound the issue: aging workforces (average age 46+) and Gen Z attrition led to 15-20% turnover rates, per our data, with recruitment CAC hitting $4,000 per hire amid competition from insurtechs. Catastrophic claims surged 35% from weather events, overwhelming manual processes and spiking loss ratios to 65-70%. Agencies in high-exposure areas like the Gulf Coast faced 80% higher nonrenewal rates, per Treasury data, eroding revenue per policy by 10-15%. KPI Breakdown: Quantifying the Losses Our analysis of 2023-2025 benchmarks highlights deteriorating metrics: KPI 2023-2025 Benchmark Monthly Loss Impact Inefficiency Indicator CAC $900 average (up 30% from 2022) $7,500/month for 50 new clients (inefficient channels) High due to manual lead nurturing; 5-7x retention cost. ROI (Marketing) 2-3:1 (down from 4:1 pre-2022) $10,000/month in wasted ad spending Negative from poor data silos; 3-5% lower profitability. ROAS 1.5-2:1 $15,000/month lost revenue Fragmented tracking leads to 20% over-spending on low-ROI tactics. Revenue per Agent $400K-$500K $8,333/month per agent shortfall Stagnant from 40-hour manual tasks; 10% below industry avg. Revenue/Cost per Employee 3:1 ratio (expense ratio 35-40%) $20,000/month agency-wide High payroll (40% of revenue) signals inefficiency. Retention Rate 82-85% $25,000/month in churn (10 clients) Data inconsistencies cause 13-point satisfaction dips. *These figures, drawn from sources like Insurance Journal and our surveys, underscore a $100B+ industry-wide revenue bleed from 2022-2025, with independents hit hardest due to limited scale. Challenges Over the Next 60 Months Projections to 2030 paint a turbulent landscape, with outside factors amplifying pain points. Economic slowdowns (2-3% GDP growth), political deregulation, environmental catastrophes, and M&A frenzy could erode independent market share from 62% to 55%, per Big I data. Our models forecast 15% KPI deterioration in high-risk regions, with monthly losses climbing to $25,000+ per agency. Economic, Political, Environmental, and Consolidation Factors Economic Pressures: Inflation stabilizing at 2.7% masks tariff hikes and geopolitical tensions, potentially reigniting claims costs by 10-15% (BCG). Non-life ROE may dip to 11% by 2025 before rebounding, but independents face 3-5% lower growth from high interest rates squeezing small-business clients. Political rollbacks under new administrations could cut compliance costs by 10% but spike volatility, raising reinsurance premiums 20% in trade-dependent regions like the Midwest. Environmental Risks: Climate events drove $357B in 2023 losses, with a $234B protection gap. Premiums in top-risk counties rose 22% (2020-2023), averaging $500 household jumps. Forecasts to 2030 predict 35% more severe weather, pushing loss ratios to 75% and nonrenewals 80% higher in exposed areas. Regional Differences: Coastal Southeast (Fla., La., Texas) faces acute adversity: Fla. premiums surged 42% in 2023 to $11K/year, with 13 insurers exiting; uninsurability risks 20% of policies by 2028, per Treasury. Gulf states could see CAC +25% from fraud spikes post-disasters. Midwest hail-prone areas (e.g., Minn.) face 15-20% premium hikes, eroding revenue per agent by 12%. West (Calif., Colo.) grapples with wildfires, with 82% higher costs in high-risk ZIPs ($2,321 avg. premium). Rural Heartland agencies, less climate-hit, suffer more from consolidation (250% M&A rise since 2013), losing 15% market share to PE-backed giants. Consolidation Wave: M&A hit record highs in 2024 (third-highest volume), with PE driving 17 new $1B+ brokers. By 2030, 20% more mid-sized independents ($500K-$10M revenue) may consolidate, per MarshBerry, slashing contingent commissions 10-15% and pressuring ROAS via lost carrier alignments. Political stability aids PE "dry powder," but independents in urban Northeast (N.Y., Mass.) face 30% higher acquisition pressure vs. rural South. Projected KPI Deteriorations KPI 2025-2030 Forecast Monthly/Annual Loss Projection Regional Variance CAC +15-20%/year $11,250/month (coastal); $9,000 (inland) +25% Southeast from claims surge. ROI 1.5-2:1 $15,000/month wasted -10% Midwest from tariffs. ROAS 1-1.5:1 $20,000/month -15% West from wildfire nonrenewals. Revenue per Agent $350K-$450K (-10%) $10,000/month/agent -12% Gulf from talent flight. Revenue/Cost per Employee 2.5:1 (expense 40-45%) $25,000/month +18% rural from M&A competition. *These trends, informed by Deloitte and EY outlooks, signal $150B in cumulative losses unless addressed. Agentic and GenAI Voice and Productivity Agents Agentic AI—autonomous systems orchestrating workflows—and generative AI (e.g., voice-enabled chatbots) offer a lifeline, automating 40-50% of tasks today and scaling to 60% by 2030. Current Benefits for Agency Owners Voice AI agents handle inbound calls, triaging claims in minutes (40% faster), reducing CAC 25% via automated lead qualification. In our trials, agencies saw 20% cross-sell uplift from personalized scripts, boosting revenue per client $500/year. Fraud detection flags anomalies in real-time, cutting losses 15-20% ($5,000/month savings). Productivity soars: agents reclaim 20-30 hours/week for high-value sales, lifting revenue per agent 15%. ROI hits 5:1 on implementation, with ROAS improving to 3:1 through data-driven targeting. For operations, multi-agent systems integrate CRM and policy tools, slashing expense ratios 10% by minimizing silos. Customer retention climbs 10-13 points via empathetic voice interactions, per Salesforce. Future Benefits and Technological Advances (2025-2030) By 2030, AI premiums could reach $4.7B annually (Deloitte), with voice AI evolving via multi-agent orchestration and Retrieval-Augmented Generation for hyper-personalization. Advances include real-time risk profiling (seconds vs. weeks), dynamic pricing via IoT/voice data, and predictive claims prevention—reducing loss ratios 20%. Agencies will automate 50%+ underwriting, freeing staff for strategy and cutting CAC 30-40%. In high-risk regions, voice agents will enable resilient quoting amid disasters, stabilizing revenue per employee +15%. Overall, expect 10-20% premium growth, 20-40% onboarding cost cuts, and 65% complaint reductions (McKinsey). Conclusion and Call to Action Independent agencies stand at a crossroads: cling to outdated models and face $25K+ monthly erosions, or embrace AI to reclaim efficiency and growth. ASNOA: KPIs for Owners 6. InsightSoftware: Insurance KPIs 7. Deloitte: 2025 Outlook 8. Agent for the Future: 2025 Predictions 9. BCG: Insurance 2025 10. AgileCap: Political Impact 11. items.rss_title: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech
items.rss_description: Friday the 13th Comes for Our Tech PaulCarroll Mon, 11/16/2026 - 17:10 When I ran the editing operation for the Wall Street Journal's European edition in the '80s, the "lockup" at midnight (or so) was frequently so chaotic that I posited what I called Carroll's law. Building on Murphy's law – everything that can go wrong will go wrong – Carroll's law said Murphy was an optimist. I'm feeling déjà vu , given all the technology-related chaos of the past week, centered on Friday the 13th, when all U.S. air traffic was shut down for hours and Microsoft's Outlook was only intermittently operating after a full-on outage the day before, for what amounts to the email backbone for the world economy. As much as there are individual reasons for those outages and other recent ones, the problems point to a pattern. The transition we're going through to a completely wired, AI world is so fundamental that two things are true: 1) We need to be a lot more careful about work like the upgrades to the FAA system, and we can head off a lot of problems if we are. 2) There will still be chaos from time to time, including for the insurance industry, especially as we start to roll out AI agents. So buckle up. Let's have a look. I first started thinking a couple of weeks ago about writing about the risks that arise from connecting everything to everything through the Internet of Things. The impetus was a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems throughout Europe – including in France, the U.K., Italy, Belgium, Sweden, Luxembourg and Estonia – followed by similar attacks on commissaries at U.S. military installations. The hackers raised the temperature inside 900 freezer units across 17 countries to as high as 120 degrees Fahrenheit, causing millions of dollars of food to go bad overnight and be thrown out. France, which suffered two-thirds of the attacks on freezers, blamed Iran, and geopolitical tensions could well lead to such attacks. North Korea, Russia and China all have active military cyber units. It's also possible that teenagers who in the past might have spraypainted graffiti on a school wall will now use AI to indulge their anger and show off in much more destructive ways. In any case, the cyber attacks show that the power of the IoT comes with a potential downside. Connecting essentially every device to every other device gives hackers more routes into systems they want to attack. And industrial systems, such as those that let supermarkets monitor and manage refrigeration centrally typically aren't built to the same security specifications that the main IT systems are. Insurers will have to be alert both about clients and about themselves. Clients may suffer theft, business interruption, claims of negligence against directors and officers, and so on. Insurers may face attacks themselves as they link to more sensors, third-party data sources, and providers of digital services such as payments. Insurers certainly make juicy targets, given all the important information they have on individuals and businesses. The Wall Street Journal published a story with the headline, " Supermarket-Fridge Hacks Show Risk of Linking Everything to the Internet" , that said: "Artificial intelligence suddenly makes the problem much bigger, because hackers are automating their hunt for exposed web connections and running searches at blistering speeds." The article adds that 20% of IoT devices already have at least one known cybersecurity vulnerability. It turns out, though, that the refrigerator cyberattacks were just the start. On Thursday, bleeding into Friday, Microsoft's Outlook email system went down. As Wired wrote in a story headlined " The Microsoft Outage Is a Warning for the World ": " The outages have caused widespread disruption to schools, courts, governments, and law enforcement agencies—plus countless businesses and millions of employees—around the globe, highlighting how many of the world’s most crucial systems rely upon technologies from a small number of tech companies. And when they fail, the ramifications can be huge." Full details on the cause of the outage have yet to be provided. At the least, it shows the danger of concentration for a key service such as communication. We've actually seen even more, though smaller, examples of dangerous concentration just since Friday. United Airlines, which controls a major chunk of air travel in the U.S. and internationally, had to delay all departing flights for more than an hour and a half on Monday because of a software issue. A technical glitch with software at Chase Bank delayed online banking and caused transaction glitches for both itself and other major banks. Concentration will only increase from here, so we need to be prepared for the fact that a single problem can cause widespread trouble. There is some speculation that AI may have played a role in the Outlook trouble, given that Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees in July and just offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 people, or 27% of its workforce, while saying the company is turning more coding work over to AI. Which brings us to the FAA communications disaster that shut down air travel for five hours in the U.S. on Friday. The current official explanation is that a single, old router in Arkansas was overwhelmed during an upgrade to new technology, but some officials initially said an upgrade to AI technology known as SMART may also have been involved. Oddly, the disagreement is very public and at the cabinet level – the secretary of Transportation insists the AI work had no bearing on the outage, while the secretary of Homeland Security has suggested at least twice that the AI initiative may have been to blame. Whatever the exact problem, the FAA issue should be the simplest to avoid. It just requires some basic hygiene. For instance, you have to give yourself a way to instantly undo an upgrade if it starts to go south. And whatever you do, you don't do a major upgrade during a busy period -- such as a Friday afternoon, when millions of people are flying somewhere for the weekend. You do the upgrade in the middle of the night, when a problem can be corrected before much of anyone notices. But people will ignore basic principles of software management, just as they'll be too reliant on single sources of key digital services such as communication and will be too slow to tackle the vulnerabilities that come from connecting to systems and services that aren't secure enough. And AI will greatly accelerate the pace at which problems surface. So we should consider recent events as warnings of future problems, not as one-offs. There is good news in the short term, though, for those of you who are superstitious types. Friday wasn't just the 13th; an astrology-curious acquaintance tells me Mercury and Venus both ended their retrogrades that day, bringing some supposed relief after weeks of celestial troublemaking. (Mercury, I'm told, can be especially problematic. It's blamed for everything from miscommunications to travel mishaps.) But both planets have resumed their normal forward movement across the sky, so astrologers give us an all clear – or at least a mostly clear, because the planets' "shadow" periods will last for a few weeks. Cheers,' Paul P.S. I later learned, courtesy of Google, that many people had beaten me to the Carroll adaptation of Murphy's law. Oh, well. P.P.S. My favorite tweet on the tech outages: "If you booked your United Airlines flight through your Chase Bank account and need to access those records on your Outlook, what do you do?" Image Paul Carroll The air traffic debacle and email outage on Friday don't just call for more careful management of our technology. They also offer a stark warning. As we’d been reporting, VIG Re saw its debut cat bond well-received by investors, allowing the reinsurance company to secure more retrocessional protection than it was originally targeting, at better than anticipated pricing. VIG Re first ventured into the catastrophe bond market in October. As we reported on October 28th, the reinsurer was initially seeking €50 million of retrocessional reinsurance windstorm protection from investors with this debut Charles Bridge Re deal. Ultimately, VIG Re experienced a positive market environment, which led to the firm upsizing its first cat bond to provide €60 million of retrocessional reinsurance protection, while also achieving attractive, below-guidance pricing for the coverage . VIG Re is clearly delighted with the experience, as this morning it hailed the fact it has secured €60 million of multi-year retrocessional reinsurance protection covering European windstorm risks, to run from January 2027 through December 2030. This four years of per-occurrence based retrocessional protection against European extratropical cyclone events, is structured using an industry-loss trigger, with industry loss events to be reported by PERILS AG. As VIG Re’s first cat bond and also the first for any re/insurer headquartered in the Czech Republic, the Charles Bridge Re 2026 transaction is seen as a significant milestone for VIG Re. Tobias Sonndorfer, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, VIG Re, explained, “Our first catastrophe bond marks an important milestone in the evolution of VIG Re’s retrocession strategy. “Accessing the insurance-linked securities market allows us to diversify our reinsurance panel, broaden our risk-transfer options and manage capacity more effectively across market cycles, supporting VIG Re’s long-term development.” The transaction, which came to market with the assistance and support of both Aon Securities and Marsh Securities who jointly acted as structuring agents and bookrunners, experienced strong demand from capital markets investors which helped VIG Re secure the slightly greater than initially targeted €60 million of retrocession at attractive pricing. Recall that, the €60 million of Charles Bridge Re 2026 DAC notes have an initial expected loss of 1.77% and were first marketed with price guidance for a risk interest spread of between 3% and 3.5%. Ultimately the coverage was secured with VIG Re’s debut cat bond set to pay investors a spread of 2.5%, so below the initial guidance range and indicative of a strong result. Wolfgang Hajek, Board Member and Chief Financial Officer, VIG Re, also commented, “This transaction adds a complementary source of multi-year capacity to our retrocession programme, strengthening portfolio resilience and enhancing our ability to manage risk and capital efficiently. “As the first VIG company to sponsor an insurance-linked securities transaction, VIG Re has also developed valuable expertise and established a platform that can support future risk-transfer solutions across the VIG Group. With this a big thank you to the colleagues working passionately and contributing on this important transaction.” As a reminder, you can read all about this Charles Bridge Re 2026 DAC catastrophe bond transaction in our extensive Deal Directory , where you can analyse details of almost every cat bond ever issued. items.title: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.original_title: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_title: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_description: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online Life & Health ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 13:16 Scammers increasingly impersonate insurers to steal identities and money during open enrollment. November 12, 2026 Image Last year, the Justice Department brought the largest healthcare fraud case in its history, which included charges that criminals stole the identities of more than 1 million Americans to submit $10.6 billion in fraudulent Medicare claims for urinary catheters. While Medicare blocked nearly all of it, private Medicare supplemental insurers paid out about $900 million. Americans lost a record $20.9 billion to internet crime in 2025, up 26% in one year, according to the FBI. Insurance fraud, including healthcare fraud, costs Americans more than $300 billion a year, and health insurance scams pick up during open enrollment, the FTC says. Seniors are the hardest-hit age group, losing $7.7 billion in 2025, up 59% in one year. In fact, Michigan officials warned on Oct. 12 of impostors claiming to be from Medicare to dupe older adults. As co-founder of Spokeo , a people search company, and former co-chair of the W3C Credentials Community Group , I have witnessed firsthand how scammers have grown increasingly sophisticated over the last 20 years. Insurance scams are evolving and costly We are seeing many insurance-related scams in 2026. Fraudsters are buying sponsored search ads with web addresses and logos that look very similar to HealthCare.gov and Medicare.gov . When Americans click on the link, they end up buying a plan that is not real insurance and also fork over their personal information, which can lead to identity theft. Even large health insurers are being duped, as the $900 million loss in the catheter case shows. The Coalition Against Insurance Fraud calls insurance fraud "the crime we all pay for," because it comes back to honest policyholders as higher premiums, which can hurt retention. In a September survey by BrandShield , 30% of U.S. adults said they would stop buying online from brands scammers had impersonated. For an insurer, that is a renewal lost to a scam it never ran. Here are three tips for insurers to help prevent insurance fraud Say what you will never do. Tell customers you will never ask for a one-time code or take payment by gift card, wire or crypto. Put the statement on the ID card, in the app, and on every renewal notice. Explain what numbers to trust and verify. Scammers can spoof caller ID so your company's name appears on a customer's phone. In every fraud alert, encourage customers to use the number on their card and check the identity of incoming callers with a reverse phone search . Report fake ads and websites and warn consumers. Search regularly for impostors using your name and report them to the FBI IC3 , the FTC , and the online platform where they live. Send alerts to customers in real time. Harrison Tang

items.extracted_text: AXA XL hires Subramanian to Alternative Capital team in London - Artemis.bm AXA XL hires Subramanian to Alternative Capital team in London 19th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard AXA XL has hired Murali Subramanian as a quantitative specialist for its Alternative Capital team in London, where he will focus on developing insurance-linked securities and capital solutions across the firm’s broad portfolio of risks. Subramanian joins AXA XL from his most recent role at insurance broker Marsh, where he served as a Vice President of Energy and Power, a role he held for over two years. He also served as an Account Executive and managed a multi-year pipeline across key enterprise energy accounts, helping to drive growth in both insurance and risk management products, while also co-leading complex placements across multiple lines of re/insurance. Before joining Marsh, Subramanian worked at Ledger Investing, an insurtech and casualty insurance-linked securities company, as an Associate specialising in casualty ILS. During his tenure at that firm, he evaluated casualty ILS investment opportunities sourced through Ledger’s broker-dealer using stochastic models and contributed to product strategy for the casualty ILS market. As well as this, he also reviewed reinsurance contracts, term sheets, and offering documents to determine whether their terms aligned with the investor’s risk appetite. At AXA XL, Subramanian has taken on the London-based position of Quantitative Specialist, Investor Relations, focused on ILS and Alternative Capital Solutions. “Pleased to share that I have joined AXA XL’s Alternative Capital team in London. items.rss_description: The Claim Runs on the Data Captured First Claims ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 12:23 Carriers investing in AI-driven claims automation face a data quality crisis rooted in fragmented, inconsistent loss documentation from the field. November 18, 2026 Image For years, loss documentation has been treated as a checklist. Get the photos, get a sketch, get the measurements, close the file. That worked when the file's only job was to support one estimate. It does not hold up now. The capture from the first visit has become the foundation the rest of the claim is built on, and increasingly the foundation that automation and artificial intelligence are built on, too. So the question that matters is no longer whether the field got good photos. It is whether the capture produced data the rest of the claim can actually use. A scan with inconsistent measurements or missing coverage does not just put one claim at risk. It becomes a data quality problem that follows the file everywhere it goes. Fragmented capture is a data problem Most loss documentation is still assembled from separate tools. Photos on a phone. A sketch in one app. Measurements in another. Each piece is its own file, in its own format, captured in its own moment. That fragmentation is where the data problems start. Gaps open between the pieces. The photos cover one set of rooms, the sketch another. A measurement in one tool does not match what the photos show. None of it was built to work together, so the mismatches compound as the file moves downstream, and a weak capture ends up weakening everything built on top of it. Carrier claims leaders feel this even though they never pick up a camera. What they need from a file is data they can trust and the full context of the loss. A folder of photos gives them neither. It shows the angles someone chose to shoot, not the loss in context, and it leaves the person reviewing the file to fill the gaps from memory. What claim-ready data actually requires Claim-ready data is not better photos. It is complete coverage the field can confirm on site, so no one drives back for the room they missed. It is consistent, structured damage tags instead of loose notes. It is measurements the estimate can trust. And it is a record that drops into the estimating platform instead of being keyed in by hand. Completeness is the part that pays off later. When the whole property is captured, affected and unaffected areas alike, the record answers the disputes that actually come back. A homeowner reports new damage in the next room weeks later. A capture of that room from day one shows whether the damage came from the original loss or from something unrelated. When the rebuild scope gets challenged, the file shows the full loss, room by room, not a reconstruction from memory. That context exists for one moment only, before the cleanup starts. You cannot shoot it again after the fact. If it was not captured on the first visit, it is gone for good. The data has to move Complete, structured, trustworthy data is still worth nothing if it sits on a field device. In a contested or high-value loss, the people who need to see the scene are rarely the ones who captured it. The desk adjuster setting scope. The examiner reviewing the file. Counsel deciding in the first week whether there is a subrogation case worth pursuing. Here is the gap almost no one has closed. The technology to capture a full virtual walkthrough on site and send it as a link before anyone leaves already exists. Used that way, the desk gets eyes on the loss the same day, approvals move faster, and a subrogation opportunity gets flagged while the evidence is still on the floor. That last one runs on a short clock. Subrogation is usually decided in the first days, and the physical evidence, a failed valve or an appliance, is often gone within hours of mitigation. In practice, this almost never happens. The contractor does not send the link. The adjuster does not open it when they do. The record sits in the field while the window that matters runs out. The carriers that close that loop change what documentation is for. It stops being an archive to pull from later and becomes a decision they can make the same day. Getting it right the first time This is where the stakes climb. Carriers are putting real money into automation and artificial intelligence to triage, estimate, and audit claims. Those systems do not learn from the active file alone. They learn from the archive. A decade of thin, inconsistent photo sets is not a dataset. A decade of complete, structured records is. That raises the cost of getting the first capture wrong, because there is only one. So the real test for capture technology is no longer whether it takes good pictures. It is whether the field can verify coverage on the spot, whether the output is structured data instead of loose files, whether the measurements can carry an estimate, whether the record hands off cleanly into the estimating platform, and whether the organization can secure it and still reach it years later. A carrier cannot operate every camera in the field. But carriers set the standard for what a loss file has to contain, and they decide how fast that file has to move. Set the standard for the data the whole claim will run on, not for the photos that clear today's file, and the record holds up every time the claim asks it to. Kayla Theriot

items.extracted_text: German Authorities Lift Threat Level to IT Security to ‘Tense to Critical’ Article 0 Comments German authorities have raised their assessment of the threat to information technology systems to “tense to critical,” noting that agentic artificial intelligence systems are providing more opportunities for attackers. Many companies and consumers had a false sense of security about the risks they faced, according to the report on Thursday by the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI). The agency issues an assessment once a year. Last year, it described the situation as “tense.” The warning comes as cyberattacks in recent months have disrupted supermarket cooling systems across Europe, French blood banks and German hospitals, underlining the threat to interconnected structures underpinning modern economies. The BSI also joined other governments on Wednesday in sounding the alarm over a critical flaw in the popular programming language Java that could allow hackers to access computer systems, the latest high-profile cyber incident in recent weeks. “Where exploiting vulnerabilities used to require expert knowledge and took a certain amount of time, attacks are becoming ever faster, cheaper, and more targeted,” the report said. The BSI Cyber Index, which measures cybersecurity threats, has risen sharply since the middle of last year, to 238 points at the middle of the year from 124 at the same point in 2025. High-performance AI models can find and exploit weaknesses with increasing speed and range and the threat took a “critical turn” in the current period, the report said. It said email-based attacks were declining as malicious actors used AI models to attack systems directly. So-called attack surfaces — the sum of potential entry points and vulnerable areas — had increased considerably as digitisation and connected devices have spread in Germany, the report also said. It warned that governments were making progress in tightening regulation of IT security but many companies had been too slow to strengthen their defenses, particularly by failing to use AI systems to scan for vulnerabilities before attacks. “Small and medium-sized enterprises form the backbone of the German economy, but often have little to counter attacks,” the report said. Operators of critical infrastructure, which have been subject to tougher regulation, are generally better protected but there is “room for improvement,” it added. (Reporting by James Mackenzie, editing by Friederike Heine and Edwina Gibbs) Related: German Watchdog Warns Some Cooling Systems Remain Vulnerable to Hacking Copyright 2026 Reuters. items.extracted_text: JPMorgan Warns That Some Vendors Were Hit by a Cyberattack Article 0 Comments JPMorgan Chase & Co. said some of its customer information may have been accessed in a cyberattack on some of the bank’s vendors. The bank said it believes, based on an investigation so far, that hackers accessed marketing data held by those companies, which may include customer names and email addresses. The bank said the issue isn’t related to an outage it faced earlier this week. The bank, which didn’t name what companies were hit, said there’s no disruption to its services and that it will contact customers who were affected and offer support, such as credit monitoring services, according to a statement Thursday. Earlier this week, JPMorgan faced an outage that affected customers, a disruption that the firm has said wasn’t related to cybersecurity. It was one of the latest in a string of digital issues that have spurred fears about the safety of technology powering some of the biggest companies. items.title: Tech Paranoia Intensifies After Outages Roil Public Trust
items.original_title: Tech Paranoia Intensifies After Outages Roil Public Trust
items.rss_title: Tech Paranoia Intensifies After Outages Roil Public Trust
items.rss_description: Technology failures disrupting everything from Americans’ air travel and banking transactions to secretive work at the U.S. National Security Agency are fueling public distrust and paranoia about tech infrastructure — even with no sign the episodes are linked or the …
items.extracted_text: Tech Paranoia Intensifies After Outages Roil Public Trust Article 0 Comments Technology failures disrupting everything from Americans’ air travel and banking transactions to secretive work at the U.S. National Security Agency are fueling public distrust and paranoia about tech infrastructure — even with no sign the episodes are linked or the work of malicious actors. Breakdowns over the past week have caused enough havoc to spur American consumers into a panic-buying spree. At Costco Wholesale Corp., surging purchases of nonperishable foods, water and battery supplies led analysts to increase its share price target to $1,150 from $1,100. Most of the company’s high-ticket generators were sold out online as of Sunday. Late night comedians have also feasted on the tech-related turmoil: Saturday Night Live dedicated its cold open over the weekend to a faux CIA meeting where an agent played by comedian John Mulaney used problems at the Federal Aviation Administration and Microsoft Corp. as a punchline. It’s unusual and concerning to have so many high-profile incidents clustered so closely together, said Joe Slowik, director of threat research and cyber engineering at the risk intelligence firm Dataminr. “We have become far too reliant on infrastructure that is shaky being more available than it is,” he said. Markwayne Mullin Photographer: Shawn Thew/EPA/Bloomberg Seeking to quell the disquiet, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump, told reporters early Wednesday that the U.S. had no indication or evidence that the technology breakdowns were related or the result of hostile acts. Taken together, however, the episodes touch on the broader anxieties surrounding artificial intelligence, including the possibility that AI tools could make it easier for malicious actors to knock out essential services or conduct cybercrime sprees. Senator Mark Warner, Democrat from Virginia, said in a statement that it appears the incidents are the “consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape.” “AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner said. In the latest glitch, a classified computer network that the NSA uses for internal communications went down on Tuesday, leaving some staff unable to access workplace systems, according to a person familiar with the matter. The issue resulted in the NSA telling some personnel to delay their arrival at the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, the person said. Computer troubles at the spy agency were joined by failures Tuesday on some Apple Inc. platforms, the latest in a series of breakdowns that also hobbled Microsoft’s software and snarled air traffic nationwide over the past several days. The episodes Tuesday capped a week of similar problems elsewhere, including a technical lapse at Chase on Monday that caused some customers’ transactions to take longer to process. The issue wasn’t related to a cybersecurity event, the bank said, but tied to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems. United Airlines also said on Monday that a tech issue impacted its departing flights, and that the problem was traced to equipment problems involving the agency’s aging communications infrastructure. A lack of quick and clear answers about the events created opportunities for conspiracy theorists and unreliable social media influencers to capitalize. Some viral posts suggested the U.S. was under a coordinated attack from a foreign — or extraterrestrial — government. Others warned that the tech disruptions signaled a kind of warning for a vague future cataclysm. At Apple, the company is working to restore its systems after an internal update caused wide-scale outages Tuesday, disrupting employee tools, retail operations and consumer services. The malfunction knocked out several internal services, including AppleWeb, the employee portal, AppleConnect, the internal sign-in system, and virtual private network access for remote workers, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Microsoft’s productivity software was hobbled for a more extended period last week after a bug caused a systems malfunction during an otherwise routine rerouting of user traffic. And U.S. air traffic experienced its worst weekend in decades after a government contractor tried to replace outdated copper wire at a remote location in Arkansas, causing a router to overwhelm others on the air traffic control network with excessive connection requests. The Trump administration is under pressure for more answers to the rapid-fire series of glitches. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told CNBC that the recent technology failures weren’t the result of a cyberattack, while President Trump sought to play down the significance of the malfunctions after being asked about them in Asia. “It’s going to be very much under control. It’s life,” Trump said Tuesday when questioned about the outages at Chase and Microsoft. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.” Even as the administration sought to offer assurances about the malfunctions, the Federal Bureau of Investigation issued a warning that cyber criminals and state-backed hackers are seeking to use artificial intelligence-powered tools to automate attacks on companies and other organizations worldwide. A Quinnipiac University poll released in September found that 73% of Americans were concerned that future systems could pose an existential threat to humanity. Nearly eight in 10 of those surveyed said they favored slowing or stopping AI development altogether to better understand the safety risks. Despite public misgivings about the risks posed by artificial intelligence, major technology companies are racing to use AI to discover and plug holes in their systems. AI tools have already found record numbers of software flaws, though tech firms say they are largely finding those issues themselves, rather than learning about them when hackers try exploiting them in attacks. For instance, Alphabet Inc.’s Google said in July that it discovered 433 bugs in its Google Chrome browser versus 11 in an equivalent update the year before. Of those, 401 were reported by Google internally, according to the company. Still, in June, the National Security Agency and the intelligence services of other nations in the “Five Eyes” alliance published a joint advisory urging organizations to, among other things, accelerate their software-patching practices. “AI is shortening the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation,” the agencies wrote. “Delays in patching increase risk, especially for operational systems with long update cycles.” Christiaan Beek of the cybersecurity firm Rapid7 Inc. cautioned that nothing in the public record about the latest outages suggests they were the result of rushed security updates. In general, he said that organizations face major risks in relying on outdated processes to respond to the surge in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and the resulting patches. “Complex systems fail in boring ways far more often than because of an adversary,” he said. “The boring reason isn’t harmless, though, and worryingly, it means the systems we rely on are fragile enough that we can bring them down ourselves, no attackers needed.” The failure of the FAA’s flight-control system on Friday apparently involved the replacement of an old telecommunications cable that triggered a cascade of errors involving a roughly 25-year-old network router. Experts say that network equipment such as routers can be finicky and surprisingly fragile technologies, as small errors or glitches can cause them to go haywire and either fail or flood their networks with traffic. In the wake of the FAA failures, the Trump administration is seeking $50.1 billion to overhaul the U.S. airspace system, citing an “urgent need” to modernize the critical infrastructure, though the effort is already facing objections in the Senate. “We have underinvested in redundancy — whether it’s an error, an update that went wrong, even a cyber incident – that can step in to ensure worst case scenarios don’t happen,” said Slowik. items.title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.original_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_description: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop' PaulCarroll Tue, 11/10/2026 - 12:55 The notion that there must always be a "human in the loop" has become de rigueur in any discussion of AI implementation in business. The cynical side of me suspects that part of the reason is to reassure everyone that AI won't lead to mass layoffs, but there are also plenty of practical reasons to have humans check the work of AIs. Or maybe not. At least not for long. A recent article in Harvard Business Review argues that human supervisors quickly become numb and simply approve the recommendations of the AI as it becomes increasingly accurate. And I think the author has a point, based on what I've seen of human/AI interactions in semi-autonomous cars. There needs to be a better way. Let's have a look. Early in the development of its driverless cars, Google gave demo models to employees. Google warned them that the AI wasn't perfect and instructed them to have their hands on the wheel, always ready to take control. That worked... for a little while. A very little while. As the AI proved to be reliable, the drivers began to relax their hold on the wheel, then started to take their eyes off the road, then began reading or looking at their phones. When the car signaled that the drivers had to take over, they needed perhaps 10 seconds to fully reengage. Given that a car going 60mph travels nearly 300 yards in 10 seconds, Google realized its hybrid approach wouldn't work and committed to producing only cars that could be fully autonomous. Other makers of autonomous vehicles, most notably Tesla, continue to offer cars that take a hybrid, human/AI approach, but I think that's irresponsible (as I wrote at length a year ago). Now, an article in Harvard Business Review offers a similar view about the dangers of having a "human in the loop" to supervise work done by AIs. The author, a senior fellow at Cal, writes: "Decades of research on automation show that better automation systems lead to worse human safety layers; as automation grows more reliable, the people monitoring it grow complacent, their skills atrophy, and they become less attentive.... AI compounds the problem. Its failures sound as confident, fluent, and well-structured as its successes.... "Even when validation works and people catch errors, every correction is captured as training data. Each exception a person handles teaches the system to handle that exception; the better the data, the smaller the scope of human validation needed in the future." The article says the lack of reliability of the humans in the loop is actually just the start of the problem. He writes: "The larger problem with the human-in-the-loop organization, though, is that the entire blueprint reads the transformation backwards. It organizes the company around the shrinking frontier of what machines can’t yet do. But there’s a larger opportunity here. Because AI removes constraints, it enables new combinations of work, new decision rights, and new forms of value. Organizations, accordingly, have an opportunity to reorganize and 'rebundle' around those new decisions rather than the shrinking residue of the old work." He goes on to lay out how to think about rebundling: "Instead of asking which tasks the machine can take over, leading organizations should ask which new roles the technology makes possible, and then redesign the organization around them." He lists several steps that can lead you to new approaches, which seem intriguing and which you may want to explore. For now, though, I just want to make the point that "human in the loop" isn't a panacea, certainly not in the long term. The reviewers of AI work can quickly become as reliant on the AI as those Google employees who found themselves with their hands off the wheel, their eyes off the road and their minds far away from driving when a problem popped up in front of them. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll An HBR article argues that human supervisors quickly become unreliable as the AI becomes increasingly accurate. items.extracted_text: Capital markets signal resilience for Lloyd’s despite rate softening narratives: ICMR - Artemis.bm Capital markets signal resilience for Lloyd’s despite rate softening narratives: ICMR 19th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard As rate softening continues to take shape across the Lloyd’s market, Insurance Capital Markets Research (ICMR) has pointed to the capital markets as proof that investors see a more resilient outlook and considerable upside potential ahead. “If only the softening market would wither. Unfortunately rate reductions show no signs of abating. The diversity of market observers’ comments range from “nothing to see here” through to “some classes are already underwater”. The truth obviously lies somewhere between these, but where?” ICMR explains in a recent article. When the Lloyd’s market begins to soften, ICMR emphasises that this narrative tends to indicate a uniform shift is in the works. However the reality appears to be different, and given the increased appetite being displayed from investors, this clearly suggests that they still see considerable upside potential even now. ICMR states that this is evident anecdotally in the number of new syndicate start-ups that have been launched over the last 12 months, as well as those preparing for a 1.1.2027 launch. Most recently, the heavily discussed reinsurance Cortina syndicate 1956 was launched by broker Aon and funds associated with asset manager Blackstone, while further funding was also used from the London Bridge 2 insurance-linked securities structure, to help launch the syndicate. ICMR noted that it is aware of 8 new syndicates that have been announced to start next year. However, while the new launches demonstrate “sustained capital appetite”, ICMR stressed that they could potentially add underwriting capacity into classes already facing downward rate pressure, widening the gap between top-quartile cycle managers and those chasing volume. Moreover, Insurance Capital Markets Research also emphasises that while direct data on rate softening is too inconsistent and client-specific to measure accurately, it instead relies on the broader, aggregate perspective of the capital markets to gauge its overall impact. “Quantitatively, it is difficult to judge impacts of rate softening on overall returns, partly because rate change information is itself anecdotal and will vary client by client, even ostensibly for the same risk profile. An alternative quantitative approach is to look at the issue from the other end of the kaleidoscope, and that is to look to the Law of Large Numbers, which in this case can be represented by the collected views of the capital markets,” ICMR explains. Insurance Capital Markets Research further notes that its RISX index has become a key indicator of Lloyd’s own reported calendar year combined ratio, predicting the likely outcome a full month before Lloyd’s publishes its financial statements. Given this, data from the firm’s RISX index shows that despite forward guidance seeking to temper expectations, market investors’ interest and appetite remains “very strong”, as equity share price appreciation is well ahead of expected returns on equity. “It should be noted that, comparing an equity market return directly to accounting RoE conflates two different metrics. Capital markets outperforming analyst guidance does not necessarily mean analysts got their combined ratio projections wrong rather, it suggests investors are willing to pay higher price-to-book multiples for balance-sheet resilience and asset leverage against broader macro uncertainty,” ICMR said. Importantly, the firm argues that this suggests capital market equity investors believe that ongoing concerns around rate softening, particularly claims that results will soon be underwater, are being overplayed and that significant profit potential remains available for the next several years at least. ICMR alternatively suggests that investors may also be pricing in some degree of rates softening but cautions that against the backdrop of wider economic uncertainty, they may feel the value creation potential of the re/insurance sector will be preserved or enhanced in terms of book multiples. According to ICMR, approximately half of returns on equity over the last three years of large profits have been from investments. The firm also states that interest rates are more likely to drift up, rather than drift down in the near term as well. “Even with a soft market decline in underwriting returns, the prospects for the sector appear stable compared to other, more fashionable sectors,” ICMR said. “Clearly, the range of individual syndicate’s performance will be as wide as it always is, as indeed will be the range of performance across RISX index companies. “With planning for 2027 underwriting reaching its conclusions, this provides a timely further data point on views on cyclicality. Because headline market aggregates will inevitably mask the extreme divergence between underwriting performance and investment leverage, granular syndicate-level benchmarking is essential for capital allocation in 2027.” Earlier this year, ICMR launched a new index to enhance its reporting for insurance investors and to also help enhance the transparency of investing into the Lloyd’s insurance and reinsurance market. The index also provides useful data to help in capital deployment decision making as well. items.title: After a Cyberattack: Measuring the Loss Beyond the Ransom
items.original_title: After a Cyberattack: Measuring the Loss Beyond the Ransom
items.rss_title: After a Cyberattack: Measuring the Loss Beyond the Ransom
items.rss_description: Getting the network back online after a cyberattack does not mean the business is back to normal. A company may regain access to its systems and still be unable to fill orders, ship products, or bill customers. For management, that …
items.extracted_text: After a Cyberattack: Measuring the Loss Beyond the Ransom Article 0 Comments Getting the network back online after a cyberattack does not mean the business is back to normal. A company may regain access to its systems and still be unable to fill orders, ship products, or bill customers. For management, that gap can represent a substantial financial loss. For an insurance claim, it must be measured and documented. The ransom demand usually gets the most attention. But the harder accounting challenge is often determining what the business lost while operations were interrupted — and how much of that loss is covered by insurance. A ransom payment has a specific dollar amount. A business interruption loss requires Robert Glasser a more involved analysis: What would the company have earned without the attack? What did it earn during recovery? Which expenses continued, which were saved, and what additional costs were necessary to keep the business operating? Answering those questions takes more than financial statements. It requires an understanding of how the company actually operates and a careful analysis of how the disruption affected its results. A Restored Network Is Not a Recovered Business One of the most challenging issues in a cyber claim is establishing when the interruption began and when it ended. The date an intruder entered the network may not be the date the company began losing business. Likewise, restoring a server does not necessarily restore the company’s ability to return to normal pre-loss operations and profitability. Technical recovery does not necessarily mean operational recovery. In my experience, operational recovery can take longer. Consider a hypothetical distributor whose order-processing system is restored after several days. Employees can begin entering orders, but inventory records still need reconciliation, warehouse systems remain unreliable, and previously received orders may need to be recreated. The system is online, but the business is not back to normal. Measuring the interruption only by the system outage would miss those continuing limitations. Whether the resulting losses fall within the covered period, however, depends on the policy. The analysis must distinguish three timelines: the technical recovery timeline, the business’s operational and revenue recovery timeline, and the period for which the policy provides coverage. Those timelines may differ because of policy definitions, waiting periods, restoration provisions, and any applicable extensions of coverage. System logs help establish when systems become available. Production reports, shipping records, order volumes, and management’s explanations show what the company could accomplish. A well-supported claim connects the technical evidence to the operational and financial consequences. Measuring What the Business Lost The next task is estimating what the business would have earned without the attack — often called a “but-for” analysis — and comparing that estimate with actual performance. This involves more than comparing sales before and after the event. A growing company may have expected revenue above historical levels. A seasonal business may have lost its busiest weeks. Conversely, declining demand or the loss of a major customer before the attack may make prior-year results an unreliable benchmark. Historical sales, budgets, pre-loss forecasts, customer contracts, and order activity can help establish expected revenue. But the budget is not proof of a loss simply because it was prepared before the event. Its assumptions must be evaluated against the company’s performance and business conditions leading to the interruption. Operational information provides an important check. Did the company have the employees, inventory, production capacity, and customer demand needed to achieve the projected sales? The calculation should reflect what the business could have accomplished, not simply what management hoped to achieve. Lost sales must also be separated from delayed sales. An order that could not be shipped during the shutdown may have been fulfilled after recovery. A delayed invoice may create a cash-flow problem without representing permanent lost revenue. Some customers may wait for their orders others may cancel or purchase elsewhere. Finally, lost revenue is different from the recoverable business interruption loss. The calculation must follow the policy’s measurement provisions and evaluate expenses that did not continue. A manufacturer producing fewer units may avoid certain material, packaging, and outbound freight costs. Rent, insurance, property taxes, and management salaries may continue. The question is whether the company avoided the expense — not whether its accounting system normally classifies that expense as variable. Hourly employees may remain on payroll despite being unable to work. The treatment of those wages depends on the policy’s ordinary payroll provisions and any applicable limitations. Minimum purchase commitments may remain payable. Materials ordered before the attack may still have to be purchased. A well-supported claim brings these financial and operational facts together, showing how lost sales, continuing expenses, actual savings, and subsequent sales recovery each affect the recoverable loss. Documenting Recovery Costs Financial documentation should begin while recovery is underway, not after operations return to normal. Management’s immediate priority is understandably containment and restoration. But decisions made during the response may later become central to the claim. Why was the production line shut down? Why was a temporary co-packer or supplier needed? What could employees do manually, and what work could not be performed? These questions are easier to answer at the time than months later. I recommend establishing dedicated general ledger accounts or project codes early to track incident-related expenditures. A running record of operational restrictions, recovery milestones, and management decisions is equally important. An invoice shows what was spent it rarely explains why the spending was necessary. Recovery costs may include emergency IT support, data restoration, temporary software, alternative hosting, and overtime. Depending on the policy’s wording and defined terms, these costs may fall under incident response, data restoration, extra expense, or other coverage provisions. “Extra expense” is a policy term, not simply a label for every additional dollar spent. A technology consultant’s invoice, for example, may include containing the intrusion, rebuilding systems, improving security, and performing routine maintenance. Those activities may receive different treatment under the policy. Detailed invoices, statements of work, and time records help explain allocations between work included in the claim and work excluded from it. The same expenditure should not be counted twice across claim components. For mitigation measures, such as temporary equipment or overtime for hourly workers to clear a backlog, records should explain the operational need and, where practicable, how the spending helped reduce the business interruption loss. Making the Claim Understandable A good submission explains what happened, how operations were affected, how recovery progressed, and how those facts produced the amounts claimed. Financial statements, general ledger records, sales reports, and pre-loss forecasts provide the forensic accounting foundation. Production statistics, order cancellations, shipping records, and restoration reports connect the numbers to the event. The calculations should be reconciled to those records. Expected revenue, actual results, expenses saved, and additional recovery costs should be identified separately. Significant assumptions should be explained — not buried in spreadsheet formulas. More documentation is not necessarily better documentation. An enormous collection of invoices and spreadsheets without an explanation may create more questions than it answers. A concise narrative and clearly labeled supporting schedules make the claim easier to review. This organization also helps address disagreements. If the insurer focuses on when a system became functional while management focuses on when sales recovered, the submission must identify the limitations that remained and explain their financial effect. Specific, understandable responses to the carrier’s questions are important. The broker’s claim advocate can help address coverage questions. Continuing losses require particular care. Customer attrition, delayed projects, and reputational harm may outlast the outage. Any claimed continuing loss must be supported by evidence connecting it to the cyber event, distinguished from unrelated business conditions, and evaluated against the policy’s terms, time limitations, and any applicable extensions of coverage. The objective is a defensible measurement of the financial loss, with a clear explanation of how the claim addresses the policy’s coverage requirements. Preparing Before an Attack Cyber preparedness is a business continuity issue. Management needs to ask: How will we keep operating if our primary systems are unavailable? An incident response plan should identify how orders will be received, employees will communicate, and essential financial records will be accessed. It should also assign responsibility for documenting operational disruption and tracking exceptional expenditures. Periodic tabletop exercises should assess those responsibilities alongside technical recovery. Can the company retrieve payroll records, sales data, customer contracts, and accounting reports without access to its primary network? Daily backups are useful only if they are protected, tested, and accessible when needed. Insurance reviews should occur before a loss. Management should understand notice and consent requirements, deductibles, waiting periods, limits and sublimits, and the provisions governing a business interruption loss and recovery costs. The middle of a cyber response is not the time to learn what the policy covers and excludes. A cyber claim is not measured simply by the ransom paid or the number of days the network was offline. It requires understanding what the business could not do, translating that disruption into a supportable financial loss, and evaluating the loss under the insurance policy. In my experience, companies are better positioned to support their claims when financial documentation proceeds alongside operational recovery — not months later. A clear timeline, reasonable assumptions, and organized records make the loss easier to explain and the claim easier to evaluate. Preparation matters as well. A well-developed and tested incident response plan can help demonstrate to underwriters that a company understands its cyber exposures and has practical measures in place to mitigate disruption. The ransom may be the most visible number. It rarely tells the whole story. Glasser is a managing director in BRG’s business insurance claims practice. He has more than 35 years of experience in financial management, insurance claims, and accounting and forensic fraud investigation at public and private companies. Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: KPMG Canada Clients’ Tax Data Accessed Amid Spate of Hacks Article 0 Comments KPMG Canada’s operations were hit by a cybersecurity breach that resulted in some client tax documents being accessed. The accounting and consulting firm said in an emailed statement that it acted immediately to contain the incident and secure its systems, and is now contacting affected clients. “We are confident we have protected our clients’ information and, based on our ongoing monitoring, the information impacted by this incident is not available online or being misused for any purpose,” KPMG Canada Corporate Affairs Manager Sonja Cloutier-Bosworth said in the statement. The incident was first reported by the Globe and Mail newspaper. The news adds to a litany of recent cyber breaches, including of crypto exchange Binance and French supermarket fridges, amid growing concern about the risks posed by hackers in an age of proliferating artificial intelligence tools. items.original_title: Risk managers needed in wider range of companies, says Sirm president
items.rss_title: Risk managers needed in wider range of companies, says Sirm president
items.rss_description: The president of the Swiss insurance and risk management association Sirm believes that dedicated risk managers are needed in a wider range of organisations and aren’t only required at companies of a certain size, while stressing that the role is still too often seen as a compliance function when it …
items.extracted_text: Risk managers needed in wider range of companies, says Sirm president - Commercial Risk Sabrina Hartusch, president of Sirm The president of the Swiss insurance and risk management association Sirm believes that dedicated risk managers are needed in a wider range of organisations and aren’t only required at companies of a certain size, while stressing that the role is still too often seen as a compliance function when it really needs to be involved earlier in corporate strategy. Speaking to Commercial Risk as Sirm held its annual conference in Bern, Sabrina Hartusch also warned that the insurance industry is struggling to keep pace with changing business risks and called for more collaboration across the industry, and with clients, to retain its relevance. Hartsch said Sirm continues to encounter questions about whether a business only needs a risk manager once it reaches a certain revenue threshold, and believes this is the wrong way to approach the issue. “What I have come across too often is the question about which size of company needs a risk manager. Is it relevant for businesses with CHF1bn (€1.1bn), or less, or more? I find this question fundamentally wrong,” she said. “A CHF100m company would not ask themselves whether to have accountants and controllers and so forth, so why does the question arise for risk managers?” continued Hartusch. While much smaller organisations may not have the resources to employ a dedicated risk professional, Hartusch said the underlying principles of risk management should be present in every business. “It makes sense to think about risk all the time at every business, it even makes sense in the local car dealer, in the local kindergarten. Obviously there will not be a dedicated risk manager at such companies, but the risk management mindset should be present,” she said. Hartusch has, however, seen growing demand for risk management expertise among small and medium-sized Swiss companies, including global businesses in the SME segment where finance chiefs are actively recruiting for the role. “That is promising,” she said. Risk management must also become more deeply embedded in corporate decision-making, rather than being treated as a reactive compliance function, according to Hartusch. She said Sirm wants risk managers to have a greater presence within organisations, helping senior executives bring together different perspectives and identify potential exposures before major business decisions are made. “I would like to see the topic being addressed much earlier in business decisions. This could help prevent having to make costly changes afterwards,” she said. Swiss companies face many of the same challenges as businesses elsewhere, including geopolitical instability, cyber threats, climate change and supply chain disruption, and working in silos remains a problem. “Silo work is still evident. If people don’t speak with each other, it is to the detriment of a company’s success and future, it is as simple as that,” she Hartusch. Risk managers must foster a mindset of collaboration, advised Sirm’s president. “The risk manager can synthesise, bringing all voices into one pot when it comes to risk,” she said. The growing complexity of business risks makes collaboration and forward planning increasingly important, Hartusch added. Companies must anticipate potential disruption while avoiding the assumption that they are somehow immune to unexpected events. The human element plays an important role in how organisations assess their exposures, with subjective thinking and overconfidence potentially preventing businesses from recognising their vulnerabilities, said Hartusch. “Preparation, foresight and anticipation skills are so important,” she said. Hartusch went on to warn that the insurance industry is not adapting quickly enough to changing corporate needs. Although insurers have made progress, the pace of change in the business world is outstripping the market’s ability to respond, creating potential gaps between the risks companies face and the protection available, she said. “The insurance industry has moved forward, however it is much slower than the business world changes. The needs of clients turn faster than the insurance companies can act,” she said. “On this, we need to work harder to make sure the insurance industry stays relevant. Risk prevention services, for example, still fall short,” she added. Hartusch also argued that companies needed to make better use of insurance policies as part of their wider risk management processes, rather than viewing them simply as contracts held in a drawer until a claim arises. Policies have multiple connections across an organisation, she said, and those relationships need to be actively managed. Doing so can also help businesses identify exposures that might otherwise remain uninsured. The risk manager has an important role in connecting those different parts of the business and ensuring insurance is integrated into the wider approach to risk, concluded Hartusch. items.extracted_text: Cat bond issuance can reach $25bn in 2026, market size to exceed $70bn soon: SCOR IP - Artemis.bm Cat bond issuance can reach $25bn in 2026, market size to exceed $70bn soon: SCOR IP 19th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard With a strong El Niño making 2026 the quietest Atlantic hurricane season since 1983, helping maintain a relatively benign insured loss environment, catastrophe bond issuance is on course for a record year above $25 billion, putting the market on track to soon surpass $70 billion in outstanding risk capital, according to a new paper from SCOR Investment Partners. Catastrophe bond issuance in 2026 across settled 144A and private cat bond deals tracked by Artemis recently surpassed the $20 billion milestone earlier this month. At the same time, we also reported that cat bond risk capital outstanding exceeded $66 billion for the first time ever . In the firm’s newly published paper, SCOR Investment Partners underlines that the unusually quiet 2026 Atlantic season was primarily driven by a strong El Niño. The firm notes that the 2026 catastrophe season has been defined less by a lack of tropical cyclone activity globally than by a striking divergence between basins. The firm stated that Atlantic activity remained “exceptionally subdued”, with ten named storms recorded by October 30th, with only one of them developing into a hurricane. All in all, the season’s Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) index stood at 19, which made 2026 the quietest Atlantic hurricane season since 1983. “The main driver of this weak Atlantic season was an exceptionally strong El Niño episode. El Niño is characterised by warmer-than-average sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. These conditions alter atmospheric circulation and can increase vertical wind shear across the Caribbean and tropical Atlantic, where most Atlantic hurricanes typically form,” the paper reads. However, the same El Niño conditions that suppressed hurricane development across the Atlantic, actively supported more active tropical cyclone formation in the Pacific. The firm explains that the East Pacific witnessed its most active season on record under the same conditions, with eleven major hurricanes recorded, but no meaningful losses seen for the insurance industry. It’s important to remember, that two major East Pacific hurricanes, Polo and Simon, threatened the Mexican government’s $175 million IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 (Pacific) catastrophe bond between mid-September and mid-October 2026, though neither triggered a payout. Against this relatively benign insured loss backdrop, SCOR IP acknowledges that catastrophe bond implied spreads declined in the third-quarter of 2026, attributing the decrease primarily to seasonal effects on secondary market prices. “Primary cat bond issuance is expected to remain highly active in Q4 and to push full-year volumes to a record above USD 25 billion. Cat bond spreads could tighten further by year end as the strong issuance volumes are expected to be readily absorbed by a meaningful amount of capital available in the market. However, continued robust issuance should remain supportive of catastrophe bond pricing levels going forward,” SCOR IP added. As mentioned, catastrophe bond issuance in 2026 across settled 144A and private cat bond deals has now surpassed $20 billion, which aligns with SCOR IP’s stance that cat bond issuance will remain highly active in the closing quarter of 2026, and ultimately help push full-year volumes to a record above $25 billion. Turning to the private ILS market, SCOR IP emphasises that while pricing in the space remains historically elevated, the normalisation trend continues on. For industry loss warranties (ILWs), indications ahead of the January 2027 reinsurance renewals point to some tightening, while terms and conditions have managed to remain broadly stable. In property catastrophe reinsurance, further rate softening is expected at 1.1, although to a lesser extent than last year. “Early indications suggest rate reductions in the high-single-digit to low-teens range. Despite this softening, property catastrophe reinsurance pricing is expected to remain supportive in 2027, underpinned by disciplined underwriting, sound terms and conditions, and generally favourable market fundamentals,” SCOR Investment Partners explained. “Looking ahead, the catastrophe bond market is expected to exceed USD 70 billion, driving the broader ILS market size above USD 150 billion any time soon,” the firm added. “Continued sponsor demand and growth across all ILS market segments are expanding the opportunity set for investors, but abundant capacity is also contributing to pricing pressure. items.extracted_text: Global Securities Watchdog Urges Immediate Action on Quantum Risks to Finance Article 0 Comments The global securities regulator urged the financial sector to take “immediate action” to address the risks posed by quantum computing, warning that blockchain systems might prove particularly exposed to the emerging technology. Quantum computers can solve complex mathematical problems much faster than today’s sophisticated computers, and could be used to unscramble conventional methods for encrypting digital information. In a new report published on Thursday, the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), which groups regulators from more than 130 jurisdictions, warned a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could have the ability to undermine critical financial market functions, like secure communications, within the next five years. Several quantum computing platforms are already “highly advanced,” IOSCO said. Experts say that cryptocurrency, which is based on blockchains secured by traditional cryptography, will be especially vulnerable to hacks when quantum computers come online because hackers will be able to swiftly break such codes. Financial firms should begin preparing now for a transition to quantum-resistant cryptography, the regulator said, including by drawing up migration plans, testing new technologies and engaging suppliers whose software, cloud services and infrastructure underpin critical systems. Blockchain systems face a tougher migration to post-quantum cryptography because upgrades will require coordination across decentralized networks, IOSCO said. Preparedness across the financial sector remains at an early stage, it added. The regulator warned that the shift to quantum-resistant security could take many years and involve significant operational and governance challenges, describing it as a fundamental redesign rather than a routine software update. Some crypto companies and blockchain developers are already drawing up plans to upgrade their networks, Reuters reported in July. Acknowledging the risks the technology poses to the public and private sectors, US President Donald Trump in June issued executive orders to bolster US quantum capability. Last year, investment in quantum technology startups reached $12.6 billion, according to McKinsey — more than six times the total recorded in 2024. IOSCO also cautioned regulators to be alert to “quantum washing,” where firms overstate the maturity or capabilities of quantum technologies.
